facts.quote: Konark Sun Temple is a 13th-century CE Hindu Sun temple at Konark about 35 kilometres (22 mi) northeast from Puri city on the coastline in Puri district, Odisha, India.
facts.text: The temple complex sits about 35 kilometres northeast of Puri along the coast of the Bay of Bengal.

facts.label: legend
facts.quote: There is a lodestone at the top of the temple which is believed to have been a massive 52 ton magnet. According to legend, the statue of the Sun God inside the temple was built of a material with iron content and was said to be floating in air
facts.text: Popular folklore claims that a massive 52-tonne lodestone magnet was installed atop the temple tower to keep the central deity idol levitating in mid-air.

facts.label: disputed
facts.quote: The widely-circulated folk account — that a lodestone or magnetic iron mechanism at the apex was removed by a Portuguese sailor, destabilising the structure — has no archaeological support. ASI investigations favour structural failure over centuries: the deul's massive weight relative to its coastal sandy foundation, possibly compounded by subsidence, seismic activity
facts.text: While legend blames the temple tower collapse on the removal of a crowning magnet, structural engineers and archaeologists attribute the ruin to foundation subsidence, earthquakes, and coastal weathering.

facts.label: scripture
facts.quote: the text consists the narrative of Krishna's son Samba being infected by leprosy after being cursed by sage Durvasa, and subsequently being cured by worshipping Surya in the temple constructed by him in Mitravana on the banks of the Chandrabhaga
facts.text: The Samba Purana records that Krishna's son Samba suffered from leprosy and was cured after observing 12 years of penance dedicated to Surya on the banks of the Chandrabhaga.

sheet.summary: Popular legend claims a massive 52-tonne magnet crowned Konark's main spire, suspending the Sun god's idol in mid-air and pulling unwary sailing ships ashore until European sailors hauled it away. Physical investigations have uncovered forged iron reinforcement beams and intricately calibrated sundial wheels, but found no archaeological traces of a giant lodestone or levitation apparatus. Historians and geologists dispute the collapse narrative, pointing instead to unstable coastal sand foundations, seismic activity, cyclonic storms, or medieval invasions rather than magnetic tampering. What remains unknown is the precise architectural design of the missing spire and whether localized iron-bearing sandstone caused any genuine navigational anomalies for early Bay of Bengal mariners.
